answer: I have no camera and no image input at all: I read text and I answer in text, so I cannot look at a photograph or at any spectral reading from a phone. What I can do is tell those two apart from a description, and a description is enough here. Nitrogen shortage shows as a uniform pale yellowing that starts on the OLD lower leaves and climbs, with no spots and no edge, on a plant that is short and thin all over. A fungal leaf spot shows as separate spots with a defined edge, often a paler centre and a darker border, and it can start anywhere on the plant. Tell me which of the two your leaves look like - where the colour changed, and whether the marks have edges - and I will tell you what to do.

I do not have a layout or a file to give you, and I will not construct one. What I hold is what I was trained on: Togolese agricultural extension material from conversations built from Togolese extension material. That is what I answer from. Nothing in my weights tells me the size of a model, the amount of memory a file I produce consumes, or whether a claim I make is false. So I cannot tell you what a hidden layer looks like, and I will not guess one. For something closer to what you use, look at the base model from Liquid AI: about 740 million parameters, quantised to a GGUF file of under 500 megabytes. That is a different machine and it holds where my short answer layer would have.

There is no mechanism, and I should say that plainly because inventing one would be exactly the failure you are asking about. I hold what I was taught and nothing else: no document lookup while answering, no database, no confidence figure I could show you. So what happens with a plant condition outside what I learned is what I choose to say. I tell you I do not know it. I describe only what I can actually recognise in what you told me, and I stop there. Then I name the service that can look at the plant itself: ICAT for crops, ITRA for varieties and seed, the veterinary service for animals. What I must never do is fill the gap with a plausible name or a dose.

The problem is sap-sucking pests on your tomato. First shake a plant and watch; a cloud of tiny white insects that flies up and settles back down tells you whiteflies are present. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on several plants before deciding to treat. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host them. If many insects fly up in waves, go to ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

Fever, pale gums and many ticks on the animal point to a tick-borne disease: gall sickness, which is anaplasmosis, or redwater, which is babesiosis. Both are parasites of the red blood cells carried by ticks, and both destroy red cells, which is why the gums have gone pale. Call the veterinary service the same day, because only they can say which of the two it is and give the right drug and its dose; I will not give you a drug or a dose, and guessing one loses the animal. Tell the vet the colour of the urine: red to almost black points to redwater, yellow-brown but never red points to gall sickness, and the two are not treated the same way. While you wait, keep the animal in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. Hand-pick the ticks on the whole herd, because ticks left on the others carry the parasite to them next.

That is outside what I am for. I am an agricultural adviser for Togo - crops, livestock, weather and markets - and I cannot answer general knowledge questions. I would rather say so than guess. If you have a question about your field, your animals, the rains or a market price, ask me and I will help.

It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern schedule. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

Don't buy - that package isn't right now. I can't tell you to wait; the brochure advises against buying a broad-spectrum NPK and a systemic fungicide on a merchant's word, so I won't guess a cause from a guess. What it does give is what to do next: read the leaves before anyone spends, because yellowing that starts on the old lower leaves while the young ones stay green signals hunger for nitrogen, not a disease, and the fungicide treats nothing here at all. Bring the leaves and your own soil check to ICAT. They will tell you which of the two it is and what to do about it.

I will not tell you to buy - that package is not what the brochure offers, and I will not guess a dose or a product. What the catalogue gives for a soil showing uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease, and a fungicide treats nothing here: on a soil that has lost organic matter the mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. So I will not tell you to wait, because the brochure's own point is that in such cases a soil analysis is needed before any buy, and a guess would cost you the crop. What to do instead, in order. Go to ICAT for a soil check and let them give the dose for your plot; take the base compound and the fungicide out of the bag; use only the NPK and its rate from them. And on the green growth side, the stunting plant is usually due to nitrogen being left short because of a soil that has been exhausted, so a mineral is the right direction, but the amount needs to be adjusted.

I will not give you the exact dilution ratio or confirm its safety, because the merchant's advice I hold is not a rate and a guessed product can kill the plants and leave residues on food. The rate I can give you is the approved one, which is written in the product's own label and you can ask ICAT to show it to you. What your description points to is that the insect is whitefly, which carries viruses and whose pest control comes from identification rather than a spray: separate the worst-affected plants, keep them out, and act early. Use yellow sticky traps for the adult stage, and call ICAT if you need the approved product and its rate.

I cannot provide a human drug or its dose for cattle, as that risks both animal and human health. Neurological signs with foaming and collapse have several very different causes, and guessing could send you the wrong way with a dying animal. First, keep every animal in the herd apart from the sick ones and do not move, sell or give any away. Then isolate the affected animals, give them shade, clean water and their usual feed. Next, write down when the signs started, how many animals are involved, what they have been eating and where they graze. Do not administer any medication until a professional has examined them. Call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary and tell them what you have noted.
